t: Introduction: topic and aim of the lesson
n: This lecture is devoted to impairment of health and death from chemical factors. Such cases occur relatively often in expert practice. Among violent deaths, poisonings rank third after mechanical injuries and mechanical asphyxia. The formation of forensic medicine as a science began precisely with forensic toxicology. The plan of the lesson is as follows: first the concept of poison, then ethyl alcohol and its surrogates, and finally poisoning with opiates.

t: The concept of poison and poisoning
n: First we consider the concept of poison and poisoning. Poison is a relative concept: it is a substance a small amount of which impairs health or leads to death. There is neither an absolute poison nor an absolutely harmless substance. Paracelsus said: "only the dose turns a given substance into a medicine or a poison". Impairment of health from the action of a small amount of a substance is poisoning. In forensic medicine, a poison is a substance that, even in a small amount, impairs health or kills by its chemical or physicochemical properties. Attention: there is a risk of error, since there is no absolutely poisonous substance. A substance shows poisonous properties only under certain conditions.

t: Toxicology and its branches
n: Toxicology is the science that studies poisons and poisoning. It has such branches as industrial, military and food. Industrial and agricultural toxicology studies causes, aid and prevention. Military and food toxicology also deal with these questions. Forensic toxicology resolves the tasks set by law-enforcement bodies in poisoning. There is another division: general toxicology studies the general laws of action, and particular toxicology the action of individual substances.

t: Circumstances of poisonings
n: By circumstances of origin, poisoning is of three kinds: homicide, suicide and accident. According to expert data, accidents make up the majority. In second place is suicide. Homicide by poisoning is rare. In homicide and suicide the poison is taken deliberately, in accident by chance. Some accidental poisonings are iatrogenic: the dose of a drug is determined incorrectly, or another substance is used in place of one drug.

t: Quick question: the concept of poison
n: We test with quick questions. First question: is there an absolute poison? Answer: no. Poison is relative; the dose turns a substance into a medicine or a poison, which is the view of Paracelsus. Second question: what is poisoning? Answer: impairment of health from the action of a substance in a small amount. Third question: which kind of poisoning is commoner by circumstances? Answer: accidents; homicide is rare. Attention: there is a risk of error. Poison is the substance, whereas poisoning is the impairment of health from that substance.

t: Classification of toxic chemicals: the general scheme
n: The general scheme of classification of toxic chemicals is given according to Popov, 1990. Poisons are divided into those acting mainly locally and those acting mainly generally, that is, resorptively. Local poisons cause necrosis at the site of contact, for example acids, alkalis and tincture of iodine. Agents of general action are divided into three groups: destructive, blood and functional poisons. Destructive poisons disturb the structure of the internal organs, for example mercury, lead, arsenic, phosphorus. Blood poisons include carbon monoxide and methaemoglobin formers. Functional poisons paralyse, excite or depress the central nervous system, for example ethyl alcohol, opiates, cyanides.

t: Subgroups of functional poisons
n: Functional poisons disturb the activity of the central nervous system, that is, the CNS, and the peripheral nervous system, that is, the PNS. The subgroups are as follows. CNS paralysants: cyanides, organophosphorus substances, hydrogen sulphide. CNS stimulants: strychnine, cocaine, opiates, cannabis. CNS depressants: ethyl alcohol, barbiturates, tranquillisers. Agents acting on the PNS: cholinergic, adrenergic and anticholinergic substances. Ethyl alcohol belongs to the depressants and opiates to the stimulants; there are no marked changes in the organs. Attention: cyanide paralyses the CNS and strychnine stimulates it; do not confuse them.

t: Factors influencing poisoning
n: The factors influencing poisoning fall into four groups: the poison, the organism, the route of entry and external conditions. Together these factors determine the degree of poisoning. The faster and more completely the poison passes into the blood, the stronger the toxic effect. As an example of external conditions, a closed, hot, humid environment creates a predisposition to poisoning with alcohol and carbon monoxide.

t: Factors dependent on the substance itself
n: We consider the factors dependent on the toxic substance itself. Chemical structure: carbon monoxide and CO2 are similar in structure, but their toxicity is not the same. Dose and concentration are important: a 3 % solution of acetic acid is not equal to acetic essence. Physical state: a gas acts more strongly than a liquid, and a liquid more strongly than a solid, because it passes into the blood faster. Solubility: barium sulphate does not dissolve, whereas barium chloride dissolves and is regarded as a strong poison. Poison is often added to a drink or food, which is the vehicle. Arsenic is potentiated in an alkaline medium, cyanides in an acid one; heavy metals are cumulated. Stability is also important: the potassium cyanide given to Rasputin in December 1916 combined on long storage with CO2, turned into potash, that is, K2CO3, and became harmless.

t: Factors dependent on the organism
n: Now the factors dependent on the organism. Weight is important: the dose of a drug is calculated per 1 kg of weight. Children are more sensitive than adults because their weight is small and their system of resistance is not fully formed. A healthy organism resists poison more strongly; in disease of the heart, liver and kidneys, resistance is limited. There is no difference by sex, but in pregnancy sensitivity increases. Congenitally low cholinesterase activity potentiates the action of muscle relaxants. Hypersensitivity, that is, idiosyncrasy, is explained by genetic features. Repeated action over a short time produces tolerance. With narcotics there is psychological and physical dependence, and if they are not taken, withdrawal is seen.

t: Route of entry and external conditions
n: Route of entry and external conditions. Poison enters through the skin, mouth, airways, rectum or by injection. The faster and more completely it passes into the blood, the stronger the effect. Substances readily soluble in fat, for example organophosphorus ones, are absorbed even through intact skin. Those insoluble in water and fat act only locally. Substances absorbed through the mucosa of the airways, rectum and vagina do not pass through the liver, and therefore act more strongly than from the gastrointestinal tract. A closed, hot and humid environment predisposes to poisoning with alcohol and carbon monoxide. An open environment, low temperature and humidity weaken their action.

t: Attention: distinguishing the action of poisons
n: In distinguishing the action of poisons, attend to the following examples. Calomel and corrosive sublimate are not the same. In the textbook, insoluble calomel is compared as harmless, and soluble corrosive sublimate, that is, mercuric chloride, as a strong poison. Barium sulphate does not dissolve in water, so in radiography of the gastrointestinal tract it is given as a suspension. Barium chloride, soluble in water, is regarded as a strong poison. Concentration decides: 3 % acetic acid is not equal to acetic essence. Concentrated phenol burns, diluted it is absorbed into the blood and injures. Dilute hydrochloric acid is used as a medicine, whereas its concentrated solution is regarded as a strong poison.

t: Case analysis: factors of the action of a poison
n: Three situations are given for case analysis. The first: a girl of 3 years, unconscious, with convulsions and frothy bloody discharge from the mouth, with suspicion of internal bleeding. Pyramidon was found in the stomach: before the fall she had taken 10 tablets. The second: a girl of 15 had a 10 % solution of Nembutal injected under the skin. After 4 ml she lost consciousness for a short time. Here the route of administration was changed. The third: in December 1916 Rasputin was given potassium cyanide but was not poisoned. On long storage the substance combined with CO2, turned into potash and became harmless. Question: in each case which factor was decisive: dose, age, route of administration or storage time?

t: Forensic diagnosis of poisoning: 3 stages
n: Forensic diagnosis of poisoning consists of three stages. First stage: inspection of the scene, review of medical records and follow-up history. Second stage: in external and internal examination of the body, evidence confirming poisoning is obtained. Third stage: histological, forensic chemical and other laboratory investigations are carried out. These three stages lead to the final expert conclusion.

t: Signs at the scene and in examination of the body
n: At the scene, medicine containers, packaging, syringes, prescriptions, vomit and secretions, and foreign odour are noted. Physical evidence is taken to the laboratory. Vomit, faeces and gastric washings are collected in a separate container and wrapped. Empty containers are also taken, since poison may be found in the rinsings. On the body, injection marks, colour of lividity, foreign odour and rigor are assessed. In carbon monoxide the lividity is pink, in cyanide bright cherry, in methaemoglobin brown. Attention: when poisoning is suspected, water and antiseptic are not used when opening the body, because the poison may be washed away.

t: Laboratory examination and the "three points" rule
n: Of the laboratory investigations, forensic chemical, that is, toxicological, examination is carried out most often. In it not only quality but also quantity is determined. If the poison is known, the "three points" rule is applied: samples are taken from the site where the poison entered, where it acted and from where it was eliminated. If taken by mouth, stomach, liver, kidney and urine are taken. If the poison is unknown: one third of the brain, one quarter of a lung, one third of the liver with bile, a kidney, stomach contents, intestine and 100–200 ml of blood are taken in a separate container. Attention: the material taken must not be preserved with fixatives, that is, formalin or alcohol. When alcohol and nitrite are suspected, the sample is delivered quickly.

t: Toxicokinetics and toxicodynamics
n: Toxicokinetics is the set of processes of entry, distribution, metabolism and elimination of a poison. The chain is as follows: entry into the body, distribution in organs and tissues, biotransformation in the liver, then elimination. Toxicodynamics, however, is the set of interactions of the poison with the organism and its response reactions. Take acetic acid as an example: the primary action is a burn, the subsequent action haemolysis, and the metatoxic action toxic hepatitis and nephrosis.

t: Biotransformation: metabolites of alcohols
n: In biotransformation the metabolites of alcohols are important. On oxidation of methanol, ethanol and ethylene glycol, substances more toxic than themselves are formed. Methyl alcohol, that is, methanol, first has a narcotic effect. Its cardio-, nephro- and neurotoxic changes arise from formaldehyde. On oxidation of ethyl alcohol, that is, ethanol, acetaldehyde is formed. Ethylene glycol itself is narcotic, and its metabolite oxalic acid has a hepato- and nephrotoxic effect.

t: Case analysis: corrosive and destructive poisons
n: Case analysis. A person drank acetic essence, 40–80 %, by mistake. Severe burning pain in the mouth, oesophagus and stomach and vomiting of blood began. The action of the poison has three stages: primary, chemical burn of the mucous membranes; subsequent, haemolysis from acidosis; metatoxic, toxic hepatitis and nephrosis. Acetic acid is strongly haemolytic compared with other acids. Haemolysis leads to nephrosis with haemoglobinuria, acute renal failure and necrosis of the liver. Attention: acetic acid belongs to the group of local acids, but is also a haemolytic poison. Destructive poisons, mercury and lead, act after absorption into the blood.

t: Ethyl alcohol: properties and routes of entry
n: Ethyl alcohol, that is, ethanol, is a colourless, volatile liquid with a characteristic smell and burning taste, and is flammable. It mixes with water in any proportion and is distilled with steam. Ethanol is obtained by fermentation of starchy products, fruit and sugar. Crude spirit is purified by rectification; in crude spirit and home-distilled vodka there are fusel oils. Fusel oils are metabolised slowly in the body, so their effect lasts longer than that of pure ethanol. Ethanol is a solvent in industry, a disinfectant in medicine, and an antidote in methanol poisoning. It enters by drinking, intravenous injection or inhalation of vapour.

t: Action of ethanol on the body and toxicity
n: Ethanol acts on the cerebral cortex. The "excitation" in intoxication arises not from increased excitation but from weakening of the process of inhibition. In a large dose the spinal cord and medulla oblongata are depressed: prolonged deep narcosis, reflexes disappear, and death from paralysis of the respiratory centre is possible. Approximate lethal dose: 6–8 ml of pure alcohol per 1 kg of weight, that is, 400–500 ml. Depending on sensitivity, strength of drink and fullness of the stomach, the individual dose is from 100–150 g to 600–800 g. According to the source, among acute poisonings alcohol is in first place, about 60 %. It also contributes to sudden death from cardiovascular disease.

t: Distribution of ethanol and the blood–urine ratio
n: Ethanol is not distributed evenly in the tissues: its amount is directly proportional to the water content of the organ and inversely proportional to the amount of adipose tissue. About 65 % of body mass is water, and in blood water is 75–85 %. For this reason there is more alcohol in the blood than in other organs, and blood analysis is important for assessing the amount taken. 1–2 hours after drinking, there is less alcohol in the urine than in the blood, and in the elimination period more. This helps to assess the time elapsed since drinking. The result is given in promille. In the blood of a dead body, putrefaction may produce alcohol up to 2.4 ‰; it is not produced in urine; therefore both are examined.

t: Degrees of intoxication (by promille)
n: The conclusion on intoxication and the lethal level is based on the result of ethanol in the blood. Degrees by promille: below 0.3, the effect of alcohol is not taken into account. 0.5–1.5 is mild, 1.5–2.5 moderate intoxication. 2.5–3.0 is severe intoxication. 3–5 is severe poisoning, 5–6 poisoning with a fatal outcome. Attention: do not confuse these two degrees. Urine and blood are examined together, since putrefaction may produce alcohol in blood.

t: Metabolism and elimination of ethanol
n: Metabolism and elimination of ethanol. 2–10 % of ethanol is excreted unchanged in urine, breath, sweat, saliva and faeces. The remainder is metabolised. A part is oxidised to water and carbon dioxide, much more to acetaldehyde, then to acetic acid. Substances such as tetraethylthiuram disulphide, that is, Antabuse, stop the conversion of acetaldehyde to acetic acid. Acetaldehyde accumulates and arouses an aversion to alcohol. Alcohol breaks down quickly during life and after death; in a body buried for a long time, unlike arsenic or strychnine, it may not be found.

t: Features of detecting ethanol in a body
n: Features of detecting ethanol in a body. In putrefaction, alcohol may be produced in the blood of a dead body: from a trace to 2.4 ‰. In urine, however, alcohol is not produced by putrefaction. In the first 2–3 days alcohol is partly broken down by the enzyme alcohol dehydrogenase. To assess the degree of intoxication, both blood and urine are examined. In exhumation, alcohol does not keep long: it breaks down quickly both during life and after death. Arsenic and strychnine keep well. Attention: alcohol is isolated by steam distillation. The iodoform reaction is also positive for acetone and lactic acid, so it is not the sole proof.

t: Chronic alcoholism and risk factors
n: Chronic alcoholism and risk factors. Repeated drinking produces tolerance: a small dose gives no euphoria, and the dose is increased. Then dependence: without alcohol, distress and a drive to drink again. Prolonged drinking may lead to cirrhosis of the liver, degeneration of the heart muscle and kidneys, tremor of the hands, hallucinations and delirium, that is, delirium tremens. Alcohol intoxication is a frequent cause of domestic, industrial and transport accidents. Most offences are committed in a state of intoxication. Attention: one textbook says a closed, hot, humid environment is dangerous and low temperature weakens the effect; in another, cold is also regarded as a risk factor.

t: Quick question: ethanol
n: Quick questions on ethanol. First question: what conclusion is drawn if less than 0.3 ‰ of alcohol is found in the blood? Answer: the effect of alcohol on the organism is considered absent. Second question: which blood values correspond to mild intoxication, 0.5–1.5 ‰, moderate, 1.5–2.5 ‰, severe, 2.5–3.0 ‰, severe poisoning, 3–5 ‰, and a fatal outcome, 5–6 ‰? Third question: in putrefaction, is alcohol produced in the blood or in the urine? Answer: in the blood, up to 2.4 ‰; it is not produced in urine. Fourth question: in the 1–2 hours after drinking, is the alcohol in urine higher than in blood? Answer: slightly lower; in the elimination period, however, it is higher in urine.

t: Poisoning with methyl alcohol (methanol)
n: Poisoning with methyl alcohol, that is, methanol. Its smell and taste are almost the same as those of ethyl alcohol, so cases of drinking it by mistake are known. The lethal dose by mouth is 30–100 ml. The retina and optic nerve are damaged, and sometimes incurable blindness develops. This is explained by the action of metabolites. The chain is as follows: methanol, formaldehyde, formic acid, acidosis and damage to the optic nerve, blindness. Ethyl alcohol slows the oxidation of methanol by about 50 % and reduces its toxicity.

t: Other surrogates: ethylene glycol, dichloroethane, acetic acid
n: There are other surrogates too. The whole molecule of ethylene glycol has a narcotic effect. Its metabolite oxalic acid poisons the liver and kidneys. On oxidation of methanol, ethanol and ethylene glycol, substances more toxic than themselves are formed. From ethanol, acetaldehyde is formed. Acetic acid causes haemolysis of red cells. This leads to nephrosis with haemoglobinuria and acute renal failure. Methanol is used as a solvent for varnishes and paints, and is found in denaturing alcohol and in antifreeze.

t: Case analysis: poisoning with an alcohol surrogate
n: Case analysis: poisoning with an alcohol surrogate. Loaders were unloading reagents in special glass containers; one, thinking it was "alcohol", hid one container and drank from it after lunch. Those who drank suddenly lost consciousness and died within a short time. The circumstances of the event gave grounds to suppose death from alcohol surrogates. On examination of the body, dichloroethane was found. Thus the picture of the event gave a supposition, and the laboratory confirmed it. Question: which physical evidence from the scene, container, residue, vomit, must be sent to the laboratory, and why?

t: Concept and classification of opiates
n: Concept and classification of opiates. Opiates are morphine, codeine, papaverine, thebaine, isolated from opium, and semisynthetic derivatives of morphine. Opium is the dried milky juice of the opium poppy, and contains more than 50 alkaloids. The semisynthetic derivatives include heroin. Attention: opiate and opioid are not the same. An opioid is a substance of different structure but acting through morphine receptors, for example methadone, fentanyl, endorphins. Morphine was the first alkaloid isolated in pure form, by the German pharmacist Sertürner in 1806.

t: Composition and types of opium
n: Composition and types of opium. Opium contains more than 50 alkaloids, 10–20 per cent of the mass; apart from the table, thebaine 6 per cent. Shares of alkaloids: morphine 42 %, noscapine or narcotine 21 %, papaverine 18 %, codeine 12 %. The narcotic action is due mainly to morphine; noscapine and papaverine have no narcotic activity. Types of opium: crude, processed, medicinal, with morphine 9.5–10.5 %, and opium dross left after smoking.

t: Morphine and its pharmacokinetics
n: Morphine is the main representative of narcotic analgesics: it relieves pain strongly and causes euphoria. On repeated use dependence, that is, morphinism, develops quickly. Peak blood concentration is at 2–15 min after intravenous, 7.5–20 min after intramuscular, and 30–120 min after oral administration. Bioavailability is 100 % intravenous and intramuscular, and 30–40 % oral. Morphine is distributed rapidly: 6 minutes after intravenous injection only 7 % of the dose remains in the blood. The amount in the brain is 2–5 times that in the blood. It is eliminated mainly conjugated with glucuronic acid in urine: in 8 hours ~50 %, in 24 hours ~90 % as glucuronide; after 72–100 hours only traces remain.

t: Codeine, heroin and other derivatives
n: Codeine and heroin are derivatives of morphine. Codeine is the methyl ether of morphine, one of the opium alkaloids. Its action is close to morphine, but it relieves pain and depresses breathing more weakly; it suppresses cough. Heroin, that is, diacetylmorphine, is obtained in clandestine laboratories from morphine by acetylation. Pure heroin is a white powder with a bitter taste. Under the action of alkali or heating, heroin breaks down into morphine and acetic acid. Therefore in examination it is often morphine, not heroin, that is found. Heroin was synthesised in 1874 by Alder Wright. Until it was banned it was used as a medicine; today it is the most dangerous widespread narcotic.

t: Mechanism of action of opiates on the body
n: Mechanism of action of opiates on the body. Narcotics bind to special receptors in the brain. As a result the centres of positive sensations are excited, and euphoria and a desire to take the drug again arise. The body has its own opiate-like peptides, enkephalins and endorphins. Endorphins are most abundant in the hypothalamus, which is the centre of emotional reactions. Five types of opioid receptors are known. The mu-receptors, responsible for euphoria, have been found in large numbers in certain nuclei of the thalamus. Attention: opiates have a structure similar to morphine; opioids have any structure but act on these receptors as morphine does.

t: Acute opiate poisoning: signs on the body
n: In acute opiate poisoning the diagnosis is made in stages. The first stage is suspicion: at the scene syringes, ampoules, a spoon, a metal dish and injection marks under the skin are found. The second is signs on the body: general asphyxial signs, that is, fluid blood, venous congestion of the internal organs, oedema of the brain and lungs, haemorrhages. The third is exclusion: there must be no other cause of death. The fourth is the laboratory: the diagnosis is confirmed by forensic chemical and forensic histological examination. The concentration of the substance helps to assess the time of last intake and the dose. The fifth is a limitation: if the narcotic has been quickly eliminated or medical aid was given, chemical examination may not find it.

t: Detecting opiates: forensic chemical and histological methods
n: Forensic chemical and histological methods of detecting opiates. To prove opium, morphine, codeine, narcotine and meconic acid must be found. For the meconic acid reaction, the sample must contain at least 0.05 g of opium. Meconic acid gives a blood-red colour with FeCl3, and the colour must not disappear on heating. Meconic acid breaks down quickly, so some authors require meconin to be examined as well. Forensic chemical examination gives the kind of substance, the time of last intake and the dose, but if the substance has been quickly eliminated it will not find it. Hair and nails show chronic intoxication, but the methods are only now being developed. Histological examination gives morphological signs; if chemistry is not done, it is the only possibility.

t: Chronic opium intoxication and dependence
n: Chronic opium intoxication and dependence. The dose is raised gradually: morphine addicts go from 0.01–0.02 g to 0.3–0.5 g. If intake is stopped, a withdrawal syndrome develops. In drug addiction the most specific changes are seen in the neuroendocrine system and the liver. In Austria about 30 % of deaths occurred at the first intake of opiates. In 50.9 % of dead addicts the cause is somatic disease. Detecting chronic narcotic intoxication, CNI, brings the diagnosis of acute poisoning closer to probable and helps to establish the cause of death.

t: Case analysis: opiate poisoning
n: Case analysis: opiate poisoning. Beside the body there are a syringe, an ampoule and a spoon; injection marks were found on the skin. In the internal organs there is fluid blood, venous congestion, and oedema of the brain and lungs; there is no other fatal disease or injury. The forensic chemical result is negative or low: the substance may have been quickly eliminated or medical aid may have been given. Question: is the cause of death acute intoxication or a complication of CNI? Which evidence distinguishes them?

t: Conclusion and review questions
n: Conclusion and review questions. Poison is a relative concept: it is the dose that turns a substance into a medicine or a poison. There is neither an absolute poison nor an absolutely harmless substance. Ethyl alcohol is a functional poison depressing the central nervous system. On oxidation of methanol and ethylene glycol, metabolites more toxic than themselves are formed. Attention: opiate and opioid are not the same. Opiates are substances close to morphine, such as morphine, codeine, papaverine and heroin; opioids have a different structure, and an action similar to morphine. Diagnosis of poisoning has three stages: the scene, examination of the body, the laboratory. With functional poisons morphological changes are few, and the laboratory is decisive.
